extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, performers, and students of humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for using and evaluating hyperbole (overstatement) and understatement/litotes in comedic writing or performance, including their effects, when they are funny, and practical checks to apply. Focuses on how magnitude, truth-relevance, audience inference, and topical fit determine effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the magnitude clearly distorted (up or down)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the statement clearly exaggerated (hyperbole) or noticeably downplayed (understatement)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the degree of magnification or minimization is evident to the audience. Examples: 'I've told you a million times…' and 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.' for hyperbole; 'It's just a flesh wound' for understatement. If the distortion is subtle to the point of ambiguity, the device will fail; if it's blatant, it signals the device to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the distortion expose a truth?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the exaggeration or minimization reveal an underlying truth or insight rather than being gratuitous?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good uses of either device surface a recognizable truth (emotional intensity, character flaw, social observation). Avoid distortions that are merely decorative; the humor works when the exaggeration/understatement reframes or clarifies something the audience already senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the gap between language and reality significant?
rubrics_metrics.description: How large is the discrepancy between what is said and the real situation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor often scales with the size of this gap: large gaps create absurdity for hyperbole (gross-out or comic intensity); for understatement, the mismatch creates dryness or a politeness/horror gap. Ensure the mismatch is detectable and meaningful rather than trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the audience get the unspoken implication?
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the audience supply the missing intensity or meaning that the language leaves out?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understatement relies on audience inference (they fill in the omitted severity); hyperbole often relies on shared sense of scale. If the audience cannot or will not supply the implied meaning, the joke falls flat. Test on representative audience members if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the distortion fitted to the topic (not generic)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the exaggeration/understatement tailored to the subject matter and context rather than a one-size-fits-all cliché?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective distortions are specific to the situation and reveal something about the topic or character. Generic or lazy exaggerations feel canned and weaken the comic effect. Aim for particulars that sharpen the contrast between language and reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction and effect (hyperbole vs understatement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which direction does the device push language, and what comic effect does that produce?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole (magnify) tends toward gross-out absurdity and heightened intensity; it is powerful in satire and tall tales. Understatement (minimize) produces dryness, a politeness/horror gap, or a tone of nonchalance/obliviousness. Choose the direction whose effect matches your comic goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for satire and audience comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the device appropriate for satirical aims and readily understood by the intended audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole is a powerful tool for satire because audiences easily recognize exaggeration and read the target. Ensure cultural/genre context lets the audience decode the exaggeration; irony or understatement that is too subtle may be misread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional intensity and tone signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the device accurately signal the speaker's emotion or feigned emotion (e.g., intense feeling for hyperbole; nonchalance for understatement)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole should convincingly convey strong feeling (anger, hunger, frustration) by amplifying scale. Understatement should convincingly mask or downplay feeling to produce a comic contrast. Mis-matched tone (e.g., trying understatement when earnestness is needed) undermines the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness mask / horror-gap (specific to understatement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the understatement function as a politeness mask or create a gap that implies something worse than stated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understatement may be funniest when it politely disguises horror or disaster, prompting the audience to imagine a larger problem. Use understatement to imply consequences rather than state them; avoid trivializing a genuinely sensitive real-world harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful distortion to redirect focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the deliberate distortion (over- or under-) redirect audience focus in a way that serves the joke?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both devices work because they intentionally distort reality to highlight a point or reframe attention. Ensure the distortion redirects focus to the intended target (character trait, social absurdity, ironic contrast) rather than creating distraction or confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of genre-appropriate forms (tall tales, shaggy dog stories, litotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the device deployed in a form or subgenre that suits its strengths (e.g., tall tales for hyperbole, litotes for ironic understatement)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match device to form: tall tales and shaggy dog stories benefit from escalating hyperbole; litotes is a classic understating form. Examples cited: tall tales, shaggy dog stories (hyperbole); Wilde's Earnest and Monty Python Black Knight (understatement). Using the canonical forms helps set audience expectations.
